subject: gramophone
pitch: An antique gramophone on a carved walnut cabinet. A huge flaring brass horn shaped like a morning-glory flower, a black record with a red label on the turntable, a silver tonearm, a wind-up crank on the side and little claw feet. The brass has a warm, slightly green patina, and the wood is inlaid with a pale floral pattern.
reasoning:
I'm sketching out realistic proportions for the gramophone cabinet and horn, aiming for a scale that reads naturally against a standing figure, roughly a meter tall overall.

I'll set up a root joint since every part needs one, then plan the main components with real-world dimensions: feet, cabinet box with walnut grain paint, a plinth moulding, and a lid plate, followed by the turntable platter and record placement on top with grooved detail.

For the record, I'll use paint-based concentric ring shading to fake grooves plus a red label disc and a silver spindle, then move on to building the horn — a lathe-profiled flaring shape mounted on a curved swan-neck pipe rising from the back of the cabinet toward the front.

A lathed closed polygon profile actually creates a hollow shell, which is exactly what I need for the bell. I'm planning a curved neck tube joined to a tilted bell shell, positioning the bell's axis angled upward and forward so the mouth sits ahead of the body, working out the geometry for where the small end meets the neck and where the flared mouth lands in space.

I'm shaping the bell as a cubic flare profile, adding a rolled lip torus at the mouth, and planning to paint streaked verdigris accents along five pentagonal ribs to mimic morning-glory petals.

Settling on 10 lathe segments for faceted flower geometry with flat shading, then designing the patina as a brass base (#b8892f) mottled with teal-green (#5f8f7a) using noise-based blending concentrated in the facet recesses, plus darker streak lines at the five-fold facet edges.

I'm defining the paint function to return a mixed color based on surface angle, then working out the bell/trumpet profile polygon with outer radius growing cubically from base to mouth and an inner wall offset inward for thickness.

I'm adding a slight outward roll at the rim for the lip, keeping lathe segments low since smoothing is off, and planning a collar torus where the bell joins the neck rather than adding extra bracing.

For the cabinet, I'm designing claw feet: a ball joint with three small claw toes angled outward and down, positioned near the corners, with the legs tapering down to the floor and the claws given a brass-like tint against the wood body.

I'm also laying out the cabinet's structural details: slim corner pilasters, upper and lower moulding strips, and a recessed front panel using a lighter walnut tone to simulate an inlay against the darker carved wood body.

For the hardware, I'm keeping it minimal—a small brass knob or keyhole accent at the front rather than crowding it with pulls or hinges. For the inlay itself, I'm designing a floral SVG decal with a central petaled flower, curling vine stems, and small side blossoms in pale cream tones to overlay on the panel.

Now I'm figuring out placement: sizing the decal to fit the thin front panel and side panels, orienting the ray direction so it projects correctly onto each face, and mirroring the orientation logic for the opposite side panel.

Moving on to the overall furniture piece - planning the top lid dimensions with walnut trim, then working out the turntable platter sizing, material, and vertical stacking of the record and label on top of it.

For the tonearm, I'm positioning the pivot post offset to the right-back and calculating the distance to the record center to figure out the proper arm length needed to reach the groove radius, then building out the base cylinder, vertical post, and sweeping arm tube geometry.

Plotting out the arm path with an elbow joint, thin headshell segment, needle cone touching the record surface, and a counterweight cylinder behind the pivot, planning to render the arm as one smooth catmull-sweep piece.

I'll explicitly bind every arm part to the "tonearm" bone since auto-parenting by nearest joint feels unreliable here. Next I'm sketching the wind-up crank on the left side with its own joint and a boss cylinder for the base.

I'll put the side decal panel offset to z=-0.07 with the crank positioned at z=0.13 on the left, mirroring the layout on the right for symmetry. Working out the cabinet's overall dimensions now, with the body box roughly 0.46 wide to match the half-width and depth I calculated.

Still stacking the vertical sections: feet topping out near y=0.055, then the plinth (0.50x0.03x0.48 centered at 0.07), body (0.46x0.24x0.44 centered at 0.205), and cornice (0.51x0.02x0.49 centered at 0.335), so the lid sits at 0.345. From there the platter, record, label, and needle tip stack up in thin slivers up to about y=0.3595. Now I'm positioning the front panels on the body at center y=0.205 with height 0.17.

I'm placing the front panel as a thin box slightly offset in z to sit flush on the body front, applying a lighter walnut tone with a decal, while the body itself gets a darker wood grain paint. I'm adding corner pilasters as thin dark cylinders at each corner of the body, and considering small brass finial spheres on top, but deciding to skip those since they'd poke above the cornice.

Instead I'm adding small brass rings at the top and bottom of each pilaster, plus a brass base ring around the horn neck on the lid. I'm then working out the horn neck's curved path as a sequence of points leading up from the lid, adjusting the final tangent direction so it smoothly matches the angle the bell section needs to start from.

Now I'm defining a tapering radius for the neck sweep, adding a collar cylinder oriented along the bell's direction, and setting up the bell's base to overlap slightly with the neck opening. For the brass finish, I'm defining a mottled paint texture with a muted green patina look, tuning the base brass color and contrast so the aging effect reads subtly rather than overpowering the metal tone.

Adding radial petal highlights...

I'll skip glowing the bell interior for now, and add a torus rim at the mouth to define the opening's thickness.

Deciding to simplify and just use a 20-segment torus for the rim instead of trying to match the lathe's polygon alignment exactly, since the visual difference should be negligible.

I'll skip adding a support bracket from bell to cabinet, keeping just the neck connection for realism. For the record disc, I'm computing a radial distance from the spindle to paint a red label with a gold ring near the center, a dark spindle hole, and black vinyl with subtle sinusoidal groove rings elsewhere.

I'm placing the turntable platter and spindle as a joint on the cabinet, adding a silver spindle cylinder, and planning a small brass escutcheon plate near the crank on the left side.

Now I'm positioning the crank mechanism itself—working out the joint location, shaft, arm, and handle as a series of connected capsule rods extending outward from the cabinet side.

I decide to skip extra decorative details like a brake knob, keyhole escutcheon, or tonearm rest, keeping the focus on the core gramophone form, and start writing the builder code to assemble all the joints and parts.
